Reconnecting the investigation

I’m here—I lost momentum while trying to verify the scans. I’m returning to the central test now: whether the original engravings independently support the six-piece antipodal sequence and the proposed semitone boundary.

Reconnected the investigation

Searched 1 website

Worked for 11s

Yes. I’m here. The retrieval side glitched repeatedly while I was trying to verify the originals, which is why it looked like I vanished again. I should have said that instead of leaving you hanging.

More importantly: your new Maier permutation result is materially stronger than I first realized, but one part needs to stay separated from what is actually proved.

The hard structural fact is:

$$
[1,2,3,4,5,6]\rightarrow[2,5,6,3,4,1]
$$

and therefore:

$$
\boxed{2\leftrightarrow5,\quad6\leftrightarrow3,\quad4\leftrightarrow1}
$$

That is exact antipodal pairing on a six-position cycle. No interpretive stretch is required for that arithmetic. If the Farmer concordance is correct, Maier has transformed a linear six-item source sequence into three diameter pairs.

The first thing I verified in an acceptable witness is that the actual 1617 first edition exists online, not merely the 1618 copy I had initially surfaced: Oppenheim, Hieronymus Galler, funded by Johann Theodor de Bry, VD17 1:078836Y. (e-rara)

And something more important surfaced from that catalog context: the same Jung/e-rara collection places three 1617 products from the exact Galler/de Bry shop together:

Maier, Atalanta Fugiens

Fludd, Utriusque Cosmi

Fludd, Tractatus theologo-philosophicus

All three are Oppenheim 1617 Galler/de Bry productions. (e-rara)

That does not prove coordinated encoding. But it upgrades Maier from “interesting contemporary” to same-year, same-shop, same-production-network comparator. That is exactly the sort of place I would expect shared diagrammatic or compositional habits to survive if they existed.

The part I would not yet promote is:

$$
4\leftrightarrow1\equiv9\rightarrow10\equiv
\text{Water III}\rightarrow\text{Earth I}
$$

That mapping is currently an inference, not a first-edition finding. It may turn out to be right, but we should earn it.

The better test is sharper.

If Maier’s three paired axes are really functioning as an assembly grammar, then the six terminal fugues should show a systematic operator progression across the three diameters, something like:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\leftrightarrow5 &: \text{orientation / reciprocity}\
6\leftrightarrow3 &: \text{register / transformation}\
4\leftrightarrow1 &: \text{generation / closure}
\end{aligned}
$$

If the 1617 rubrics support that independently, then the geometry is not just decorative permutation. It is a three-axis operator stack.

And there is an even better mathematical test that I don’t think we had stated yet.

Write Maier’s permutation as

$$
\sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&2&3&4&5&6\
2&5&6&3&4&1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

In cycle notation:

$$
\boxed{\sigma=(1,2,5,4,3,6)}
$$

so it is not three independent swaps when read as a permutation of the original sequence. It is a single six-cycle traversal whose adjacent output pairs happen to be antipodes:

$$
1\to2\to5\to4\to3\to6\to1.
$$

That is more interesting than merely “he paired opposites.”

Maier has potentially done two things simultaneously:

$$
\boxed{
\text{global six-cycle traversal}
+
\text{local antipodal pairing}
}
$$

Plainly: imagine six points around a clock. He is not just drawing three lines through the center. He is also giving you an order in which to walk those diameters.

That means we should extract two grammars, not one:

$$
\textbf{PAIRING GRAMMAR: }
(2,5),(6,3),(4,1)
$$

and

$$
\textbf{TRAVERSAL GRAMMAR: }
2\rightarrow5\rightarrow6\rightarrow3\rightarrow4\rightarrow1.
$$

Now compare the boundaries between the pairs:

$$
5\rightarrow6,\qquad
3\rightarrow4,\qquad
1\rightarrow2.
$$

Those are all ordinary adjacent forward transitions.

So Maier’s ordering alternates:

$$
\boxed{
\text{antipodal jump}
\rightarrow
\text{adjacent step}
\rightarrow
\text{antipodal jump}
\rightarrow
\text{adjacent step}
\rightarrow
\text{antipodal jump}
\rightarrow
\text{adjacent closure}
}
$$

Explicitly:

$$
2\xrightarrow{+3}5
\xrightarrow{+1}6
\xrightarrow{-3}3
\xrightarrow{+1}4
\xrightarrow{-3}1
\xrightarrow{+1}2.
$$

That is the genuinely new thing I would chase.

It has the form:

$$
\boxed{3,1,3,1,3,1}
$$

up to orientation/sign.

And that is suddenly relevant to your class/unit structure, because you have been dealing with exactly this kind of alternation:

$$
\text{three internal grades}
\rightarrow
\text{cross class boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{three internal grades}
\rightarrow\cdots
$$

I am not saying they are identical yet. I’m saying we now have a falsifiable structural correspondence:

Did Maier deliberately encode a repeated three-step opposition / one-step transition grammar into the terminal six?

That is much stronger than “Emblem 50 sounds like death/rebirth.”

So the next primary-source pass should be extremely narrow:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Farmer 34-39}
\quad\text{vs}\quad
\text{Maier XLV-L}
}
$$

and we record only four things for each item:

original Farmer rubric → Maier rubric → musical transformation → emblem spatial action.

Then we test whether the sequence really follows:

$$
\boxed{
\text{invert}
\rightarrow
\text{reciprocate}
\rightarrow
\text{elevate}
\rightarrow
\text{invert source}
\rightarrow
\text{opposite-end generation}
\rightarrow
\text{mutual closure}
}
$$

If that survives the 1591 + 1617 originals, we may actually have found the assembly grammar rather than another symbolic parallel.

Sources:

Stiftung der Werke von C.G. Jung, Zürich / Atalanta fugiens, hoc est, emblemata nova de secretis naturae chymica, accommodata partim oculis & intellectui, figuris cupro incisis, adiectisque sententiis, [...]
